## [2026-10-27](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-27.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [SGLang Security Update: Improving Request Isolation](<https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-10-26-cf-security>)

SGLang and Cloudflare disclose how rejected requests and asynchronous KV transfers could break request isolation in disaggregated serving, and explain admission checks and deferred cache release. The operational lesson is that request termination does not end remote memory access: safe reuse needs trustworthy drain accounting, with explicit limits on timeout-based release.

**Published:** 2026-10-26 · **First seen:** 2026-10-27T10:07:17.407Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Disaggregated Serving, KV Lifetime, Request Isolation, Failure Handling

[Blog](<https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-10-26-cf-security>) · [Code](<https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35049>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. Complete coordinated October26 reports, reproduction README and relevant implementation changes inspected. Cloudflare identifies155 affected GLM-5.3 responses during August27–September9; the immediate rejection bug is distinct from the related abort-transfer race. SGLang retains cache slots, request rows and metadata until all required drain acknowledgements or timeout. Across21 two-H100 runs, throughput deltas were within±2% with confidence intervals spanning zero. This is a new disclosure and integrated analysis; patches and the October11–12 reproducer were public earlier.

**Limitations:** Timeout expiry does not prove outstanding writes stopped; failed sends must not acknowledge drain. The controlled harness deliberately widens a race and does not estimate production frequency. Optional transfer checksums cover a particular handoff, not all future reads or model architectures. Neither small performance tests nor reproduced cases establish universal tenant isolation. No new October26 implementation release is claimed.

### [More Than DeepInfer: What SGLang Delivers](<https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-10-24-dsv41-deepinfer/>)

SGLang documents its integration of DeepSeek’s fused kernels, direct peer reads for sharded Engram tables and bounded replay, and releases a pinned comparison against DeepInfer. The tested synthetic workloads show near parity with modest SGLang gains at some batch sizes, while the accompanying commands expose configuration and timing differences that matter when translating engine benchmarks into serving decisions.

**Published:** 2026-10-24 · **First seen:** 2026-10-25T09:59:27.402Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Engine Benchmarks, Expert Parallelism, Fused Kernels, Reproducibility

[Blog](<https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-10-24-dsv41-deepinfer/>) · [Code](<https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang>) · [Project](<https://gist.github.com/sglang-bot/f03d7d0dd268b0386177eb2ef09f8b3b>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. The October 24 measured comparison reuses older integrations; its reproduction gist was created October 24 at 10:24 UTC. Matched four-GPU GB300/B300 prefill reaches at most 1.039× throughput versus each point’s fastest tested DeepInfer configuration. On 64 GB300 GPUs, decode steps are 1.1–7.4% shorter at 16–256 requests/GPU and 0.4% longer at eight.

**Limitations:** Balanced routing and static verification are forced; rates assume 3.25 accepted tokens/step. Engines differ in timing windows, Engram placement and draft redundancy. These are synthetic engine-step results, not natural acceptance, quality equivalence, production reliability or end-to-end service gains. Some flags are non-default; code was inspected, not executed.

## [2026-10-17](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-17.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [SGLang Powers Beam in Production](<https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-10-16-beam>)

SGLang integrates Beam's hybrid sliding-window and full-attention mixture-of-experts model with fused precision-sensitive operations and a jointly budgeted target-and-drafter cache for blockwise speculative decoding. The report explains how cache reuse, draft-memory placement and supported parallel layouts fit together for long-context agents, with public serving recipes and replay scripts that separate simulated acceptance from natural-workload measurements.

**Published:** 2026-10-16 · **First seen:** 2026-10-17T10:04:34.136Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Hybrid Attention, Speculative Decoding, KV Memory, Serving Recipes

[Blog](<https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-10-16-beam>) · [Code](<https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/bench-openhands-gb300-sweep-beam/benchmark/beam_openhands>) · [Project](<https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Reflection/Beam-1_0>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. Read the full October 16 report, including target/draft cache placement, DFlash2 with attention data parallelism, heterogeneous TP transfer, precision/fusion gates and the reproduction appendix. The public benchmark branch, serving cookbook and PRs 40331/40492/40909 were retrieved. Beam has 501B total/23B active parameters, hybrid attention, FP32 routing and rounded scaled residuals. On four GB300 GPUs, the OpenHands NVFP4 TP4 replay uses 13 turns, about 74K initial tokens, about 220 output tokens per turn and approximately 92% prefix-cache hits; its 127.6K total token/s/GPU headline at concurrency 32 uses fixed simulated acceptance length four. The separate AgentX replay reports 83,504 total token/s/GPU and 43.9 P90 token/s/user at concurrency 96. These are distinct workloads, not an engine leaderboard.

**Limitations:** Total throughput includes cached input tokens and is not newly computed or output-token throughput. OpenHands uses simulated acceptance with real draft tokens, so it does not measure natural acceptance or model accuracy; AgentX has a different workload and latency percentile. Shared draft placement excludes HiCache, host retraction and DCP; private fallbacks and startup gates apply, and draft capture requires PP=1. BF16 and dynamic FP8 do not use the NVFP4 MegaMoE extension. TPU recipes are forthcoming. Production-API use is author-reported rather than independent reliability evidence. Miles training results are separate from serving quality, and no author code or model experiment was executed.

## [2026-10-14](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-14.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18451>)

FastEEP resizes expert-parallel MoE serving instances by reusing worker processes, communication structure and address-stable runtime state while changing which GPUs actively participate. This lets a running service release or reacquire individual GPUs with shorter reconstruction delays; the authors report 4.5–11.7x faster resizing than their vLLM Elastic EP baseline on supported comparisons.

**Published:** 2026-10-13 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:36:43.065Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** MoE Serving, Elastic Expert Parallelism, Runtime State Reuse

**Public availability:** 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18451>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3–6 describe persistent-parent NCCL subgroups, NIXL peer masks, CUDA virtual-memory offload and coordinated worker transitions. Six MoE models are evaluated on two eight-H20-3e nodes with NVLink and 400-Gbps RDMA; resizing takes 4.2–13.4 seconds, while the compared vLLM Elastic EP takes 36.4–92.0 seconds. ShareGPT experiments also measure service interruption, distinct from overall scaling latency.

**Limitations:** This is a 16-GPU evaluation, not demonstrated hundred-rank scaling. Expansion remains bounded by the initialized maximum topology and available memory; dormant state consumes host memory. Resizing still interrupts token output. The Elastic EP baseline cannot run two of the six models, so its speedup range excludes those comparisons. A specific open-source repository or PR was not verified.

### [Taking Tokenization off the Host for Agentic LLM Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13325>)

GraphTok captures supported BPE-tokenizer operations in a reusable CUDA graph while preserving reference token IDs and routing small inputs to a CPU engine. Its new paper evaluates how tokenization affects long-context serving, separating gains in a real vLLM instance from the capacity of a shared Dynamo frontend.

**Published:** 2026-10-09 · **First seen:** 2026-10-12T10:04:28Z · **Novelty:** material-update · **Tags:** Tokenization, CUDA Graphs, Serving Frontends

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13325>) · [Code](<https://github.com/Msiavashi/GraphTok>) · [Project](<https://msiavashi.github.io/GraphTok/>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. On one H100 NVL, replacing stock vLLM tokenization lowers cold-cache mean TTFT only 2–4%, but gives 2.06–2.43× gains with 99% prefix reuse. A controlled Dynamo frontend sustains 518 versus gigatoken's 296 requests/s for 121K-token prompts under a 2-second P99 target.

**Limitations:** Dynamo uses simulated GPU workers: this is frontend capacity, not a measured 56-GPU serving deployment. Five tokenizer configurations, one GPU type and limited repeated trials; optimized CPU tokenization is close in the small vLLM experiment. Qwen normalization remains host-side.

**Update:** 2026-10-12: the newly announced paper supplies detailed serving experiments and controls beyond the implementation descriptions on GraphTok's October 9 first-release changelog and project page. The code's exact release time is unavailable, so no in-window first-release claim is made. Paper-update availability is inferred as October 12 00:00 UTC from https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/new and https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html; original v1 submission remains October 9. ### [Zepp: Accelerating Distributed MoE Serving under Relaxed Balance Constraints](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11158>)

Zepp combines locality-aware expert placement and routing with traffic splitting, node-local aggregation and overlapping execution to reduce communication in distributed MoE serving. Allowing bounded load imbalance avoids some remote transfers and expert-weight movement while preserving the model's logical expert choices.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-09T10:07:33Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** MoE, Expert Parallelism, Communication, Serving

**Public availability:** 2026-10-09T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/new>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 6.1–6.4 report a 1.86× geometric-mean MoE-layer speedup over the fastest compared baseline across 4–16-node configurations. A separate Qwen3-30B SGLang experiment reports 1.32–1.92× prefill throughput and 1.04–1.57× decode speedup.

**Limitations:** Layer tests replay profiled routing traces; end-to-end gains use a separate all-gather/GEMM/reduce-scatter baseline without overlap. ### [Session-Aware Agentic Inference with NVIDIA Dynamo](<https://pytorch.org/blog/session-aware-agentic-inference-with-nvidia-dynamo/>)

Dynamo carries session identity into opt-in routing and admission, allowing serving policies to track agent working sets across tool calls. Deferring sessions at tool boundaries can reduce repeated prefill under memory pressure, while experimental cache indexing and proposed cache hints extend the design toward shared KV storage.

A separate Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B rollout test on eight H20-3e GPUs reports 11.0–14.6% higher model-token throughput at concurrency 192–256 versus VERL's global load balancer. Conservatively labeled newly discovered because the source exposes an October 8 date without an exact posting time; this is a new technical report on existing software, not a new software-release claim.

## [2026-10-05](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-05.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [AFORE: Attention-FFN Disaggregation with Overlapped Reconfiguration of Experts](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03203>)

AFORE uses the upcoming microbatch's actual expert-routing demand to rebalance expert replicas in serving systems that separate attention from feed-forward computation. By copying expert weights while earlier microbatches run and accounting for exposed migration cost, it reduces expert bottlenecks without placing every reconfiguration on the request's critical path.

**Published:** 2026-10-02 · **First seen:** 2026-10-05T10:03:36Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** MoE Serving, Attention-FFN Disaggregation, Expert Placement

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03203>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Original v1 was submitted October 2 at 12:20:29 UTC; the October 5 announcement list and official schedule place public release at October 5 00:00 UTC, inside the main window. The older submission date is retained with the legacy newly-discovered label. Sections 7.1–7.2 test GLM-4.5-Air on 16 A100 GPUs across four dynamic workloads, reporting 10.1–17.6% higher output throughput and 7.1–9.5% lower P95 inter-token latency than the strongest competing baseline for each workload.

**Limitations:** Evaluation uses one model and two nodes. Expert replicas require spare memory, and successful overlap depends on pipeline timing and interconnect bandwidth; the observed hidden migrations are not a general guarantee. The larger expert-parallel scheduling study is trace based. No public AFORE implementation was verified, and no results were reproduced.

Retire adds execution versions to a serving stack so an agent's superseded work loses permission to publish results or install cached state. Coordinating cancellation with reuse of a verified context prefix makes instruction changes faster in the tested settings.

Vosti combines a formally verified inference engine with checked GPU-kernel contracts so batching, prompt chunking, and cache reuse preserve identical output logits under a fixed deployment configuration. It provides a foundation for reproducible serving and debugging when scheduling changes would otherwise alter a model's numerical behavior.

**Published:** 2026-09-30 · **First seen:** 2026-10-02T15:33:57Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Deterministic Inference, Formal Verification, KV Cache

Catch-up discovery: v1 was submitted September 30 at 04:58:09 UTC and appears in arXiv's October 1 announcement list; the standard announcement schedule implies October 1 at 00:00 UTC availability. The authors verify engine invariants and kernel contracts and report 5,488 matching logit comparisons across seven Llama/Gemma models, with performance measured on one H200.

**Limitations:** The proof establishes determinism, not model correctness or cross-hardware reproducibility, and trusts compiler/runtime boundaries. SpecScale prunes uncompetitive reasoning branches early, shares computation between identical prefixes, and batches process-reward verification across requests. ### [SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37626>)

SPLASH changes attention parallelism while requests are running by reusing resident weights and KV caches, transferring missing state in the background, and switching at a batch boundary. This lets serving systems adapt to changing concurrency and context lengths; its additional ownership layout stores attention weights and each request's cache without replicating either.

### [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180>)

PagedAttention stores key-value caches in dynamically allocated blocks, allowing vLLM to avoid large contiguous reservations and share cached state across related sequences. More efficient memory use permits larger concurrent batches, making this a foundational open reference for high-throughput language-model serving.

## [2026-09-29 — Landscape baseline](../../../landscape/2026-09-29.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670>)

DistServe runs prompt prefill and token decoding on separate GPUs and independently chooses their resource allocations and parallelism. It increases the number of requests served within both first-token and per-token latency targets, establishing a practical foundation for disaggregated inference.

**Published:** 2024-01-18 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T04:13:56.564Z · **Novelty:** baseline · **Tags:** Prefill Decode Disaggregation, Serving, Latency SLO

**Positioning:** established-method

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670>) · [Code](<https://github.com/LLMServe/DistServe>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The OSDI work evaluates OPT-13B/66B/175B across chat, code, and summarization workloads on 32 A100 GPUs, with bandwidth-aware placement and ablations of the disaggregation design.

**Limitations:** Results use historical engines, synthetic arrival times, and workload-specific latency targets. KV transfers need sufficient bandwidth, and the prototype leaves advanced preemption and fault tolerance to future work.
